prize_parts.citation: For empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wages, and on the persistence of workers' and regions' adjustment costs.

statement.case_for: I am changing my preferred configuration from B018 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) to B036 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson). The reason is attribution, not the opening counts. In round 1 I conceded that B018's credit is spread over at least eight serious contributors, and that any three-name cut would be hard to defend as the discovery rather than an arbitrary choice. Colleagues who also rate B018 highly (Andersson, Hassler, Boppart) reached the same view independently. I have not found an answer to it. I still think the scientific importance and maturity of the New Keynesian framework are very high, and I would not oppose it. But I cannot say which three names the Committee could defend, and I cannot resolve Taylor versus Galí as the third name from the evidence supplied. B036 does not have that problem. The local-labour-market and import-exposure programme is jointly authored by Autor, Dorn and Hanson. It asks a first-order question about who bears the adjustment costs of trade and technology, and it uses transparent designs that others could criticise and did. The core papers are about a decade old. Work on shift-share identification, persistence and automation has qualified the magnitudes but has not overturned the central finding of concentrated and persistent local adjustment costs. That is the kind of testing I want to see before a prize. I would anchor the citation on the evidence on exposure and adjustment, state no effect size, and say openly that it does not rule on the origins of the task framework.
statement.case_against: The shift-share exposure measures, the long-run size and persistence of the effects, and the split between trade and automation remain debated. A citation worded around evidence on exposure and adjustment does not fully answer this, though it limits the claim. The ballot entry bundles two strands, the task and skill-bias literature and the trade-shock evidence. A trio centred on the second leaves Katz and the task lineage uncredited, and part of that lineage involves Acemoglu (recognised in 2024) and Levy and Murnane. The 2021 and 2023 labour prizes and the 2024 technology and institutions prize make some overlap with recent recognition unavoidable. B018, B047 and B034 each have a cleaner or older claim to maturity in different respects, and a member who weights theoretical foundations over design-based evidence could reasonably rank them higher. My own changing view also shows how sensitive the choice is to how attribution is weighed.

responses.point: Andersson ranked B018 first in the opening and now keeps it as an alternative because of the attribution cap. He would support Calvo, Taylor and Woodford if the Committee judges that core clean enough, and he does not think the first-place count settles the question.
responses.response: We reached the same conclusion on B018 from the same difficulty. I do think Calvo's pricing device, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's synthesis are a coherent division of credit. What I cannot show is that the Committee could defend leaving out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, who made the framework empirically operational. Since you do not claim it is settled either, I have stopped treating it as my preferred part. I agree with your point that the B036 citation should be worded around exposure and adjustment evidence, and I do not accept the objection that the two strands cannot be bundled. Autor spans both. I would still keep the credited scope on the empirical programme and not on the task theory.

responses.point: Hassler is the chair and prefers B036. He reasons that the attribution is the cleanest among the leading candidates, and he says any three-name B018 credit looks like an arbitrary cut. He also wants the citation anchored on empirical evidence about trade and labour-market adjustment, not a general theory of technology.
responses.response: I accept the attribution point against B018 and have moved on it. I do not adopt your reading of the post-2008 and 2021-23 record as a reason to discount the framework, because I see that record as testing and extending it more than displacing it. That argument is separate from my change. I changed because the credit cannot be cut cleanly, not because the framework's standing has dropped. I agree on the citation: the evidence on adjustment should be what the prize credits. I also note that you and I are frequent co-authors. That is a collegial tie and not a reason for me to follow your ranking, and I have tried to reach this view from the written arguments.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B036 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He argues the citation should state its scope openly so that it is not read as a verdict on the technology strand. He also thinks the persistence and magnitude debate does not count against maturity.
responses.response: Your scope point persuaded me in round 1 and I would carry it into the drafting. The citation should say what it credits (evidence on import competition, technological change and local labour-market adjustment) and should not imply a ruling on who originated the task framework. I agree the magnitude debate is not an argument against maturity, since prizes have often gone to work whose size estimates stayed contested while the central discovery was established. Where I would be more cautious than you is on how firmly the evidence supports persistence. The strongest claim the work supports is that local adjustment was slow and costly, and that is the claim I would want the citation to make.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson moved from Autor, Katz and Hanson to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. She says the Dorn omission is the harder one to defend. She also says the Committee should state what the task framework adds beyond the work recognised in 2023 and 2024, and that the citation should not rest on one specification.
responses.response: My opening trio was Autor, Katz and Hanson, and your argument is the reason I have dropped Katz. Dorn co-authored the foundational China-shock papers, while Katz's skill-premium and education-technology work is an older and separate achievement. On the Committee's question, I cannot name a specific thing the task strand adds to what the 2023 and 2024 prizes covered, so I do not propose crediting it in this configuration. I should disclose that my own capital-skill complementarity work with Ohanian, Ríos-Rull and Violante is in the skill-premium lineage that the Katz question touches. That is a further reason for me not to build the citation on that strand. I share your preference for a citation that does not depend on one instrument.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 seventh and prefers B020. He doubts that the maturity bar is met because identification, persistence and magnitude are still debated. He would not oppose B036 and names it as an alternative.
responses.response: Your maturity worry is the main substantive reservation I have about B036, and I do not think it is fully answered. My reading is that a decade of replication and hostile re-examination has established the existence and local concentration of the adjustment costs even though their long-run aggregate size is unsettled. That is enough for a discovery-based citation if it makes no claim about magnitude. I agree that B020 has strong maturity and policy use. My difficulty there is the one you concede, that credit divides between the demand-estimation core and the dynamic-oligopoly strand and that Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin have claims. I have therefore left it outside my alternatives. If the Committee chooses to weigh methods prizes equally with substantive ones, I would want a tighter attribution argument than I have seen.

uncertainties: Whether the shift-share identification critiques and the evidence on long-run persistence support a lasting discovery or a contested estimate. I have no specific finding that I know would change my view, and I rely on colleagues' descriptions of the replication record.
Whether leaving out Katz and the task lineage, part of which involves Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, is an acceptable attribution cost, and whether the citation wording can keep that scope clear.
How much room the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes leave for another award on labour markets, technology and trade.
Whether my move away from B018 is too driven by the three-name cap. A broader or differently structured credit for the New Keynesian framework might change my assessment, and I cannot test that here.
I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files, with no independent verification of credit attributions.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson appears in my supplied profile. I disclose that my research in macroeconomic theory is adjacent to B018, which is now an alternative. My capital-skill complementarity and investment-specific technological change work (with Ohanian, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood and Hercowitz) is adjacent to the skill-premium strand of B036, which I leave outside the credited scope. My climate-economy and political-economy-of-growth work is adjacent to B047, another alternative. I am a frequent co-author of colleagues Boppart and Hassler (the chair) and an IIES colleague of both. I note these as disclosures and I do not adjudicate them.
